title: Sony takes its Walkman abroad
what: Sony began selling its Walkman outside Japan in February. The pocket cassette player cannot record: it only plays music, through light headphones, while you walk. In Japan, where it went on sale in July 1979 for about 33,000 yen, it sold more than 30,000 in its first two months, against the 5,000 a month Sony had planned. In some countries it is sold under other names, such as Stowaway in Britain and Soundabout in America.
why: The gadget of the early 1980s and the start of private, portable music; Sony's signature product of the decade.

title: Riots at Zurich's opera house: 'Züri brännt'
what: On the night of 30 to 31 May several hundred young people clashed with police in front of the Zurich opera house, joined by a crowd coming from a Bob Marley concert. The city council had just approved 60 million francs to renovate the opera house while turning down the young people's demand for an autonomous youth centre. Students filmed the first night of rioting.
why: Switzerland's youth revolt of 1980 to 1982: the parents of the game's teenagers may have been there; it led in time to spaces such as the Rote Fabrik.

title: Moscow Olympics: the Swiss compete under the Olympic flag
what: The Summer Olympics opened in Moscow on 19 July without the United States and dozens of other countries, which boycott the Games over the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Only 80 nations take part. Switzerland sent 73 athletes but, in partial support of the boycott, marched under the Olympic flag instead of its own. Robert Dill-Bundi won gold in the 4,000 metres cycling pursuit and Jürg Röthlisberger in judo.
why: Sport as Cold War politics, and the first Swiss Olympic moment of the game.

title: Saturday night TV: 'Wetten, dass..?' starts
what: On 14 February the German channel ZDF broadcast the first 'Wetten, dass..?' (Want to bet?), a Saturday-evening show made together with Austria's ORF and Swiss television. Ordinary people bet that they can do something odd or remarkable, and celebrity guests guess whether they will manage. The host and inventor is Frank Elstner.
why: The Saturday-evening family show of German-speaking Europe for three decades, watched in Swiss living rooms.

title: The Rubik's Cube craze
what: In March a speedcubing championship organised by the Guinness Book of Records was held in Munich, and the Rubik's Cube was on the cover of Scientific American. The Hungarian puzzle, invented by Ernő Rubik, went on sale in West Germany in June 1980 and won a special prize of the German Spiel des Jahres award. Shops cannot get enough of it, and books explaining how to solve it are selling well; most people manage only one or two sides.
why: The toy of the early 1980s; a symbol of the decade for parents and grandparents alike.

title: Swiss voters write equal rights for women into the constitution
what: On 14 June Swiss voters approved an article in the federal constitution establishing equal rights for men and women. Swiss women have had the vote at the federal level only since 1971.
why: A quiet change in daily life: equal pay and family law follow slowly, which is why women strike on its tenth anniversary in 1991.

title: Charles and Diana marry before a world audience
what: Prince Charles, heir to the British throne, married Lady Diana Spencer at St Paul's Cathedral in London on 29 July. Two million people lined the route, and the ceremony was watched on television by an estimated 750 million people around the world.
why: The 'wedding of the century', a television event across Europe; Diana stays in the news until 1997.

title: Italy win the World Cup in Spain
what: Italy beat West Germany 3-1 in the World Cup final in Madrid on 11 July, with goals from Paolo Rossi, Marco Tardelli and Alessandro Altobelli. It is Italy's third title. Rossi was named the tournament's top scorer and best player.
why: A World Cup that Ticino and the Italian community in Switzerland celebrated in the streets.

title: The compact disc arrives in Europe
what: In March the compact disc and its players went on sale in Europe and America. Sony launched the format in Japan in October 1982 with its CDP-101 player at 168,000 yen; its partner Philips now brings its own player to Europe. A CD holds music as digital data read by a laser, without the hiss and scratches of tape and vinyl. Players and discs are still expensive.
why: The CD replaces vinyl over the decade and fills Sony's and the record industry's coffers.

title: The first mobile phone network opens in Chicago
what: The first call on a commercial cellular network was made in Chicago on 13 October, after the US regulator approved Motorola's handheld DynaTAC phone in September. Until now mobile phones have mostly been heavy sets built into cars; in Switzerland the PTT's portable Natel B phone weighs 12 kilograms and comes in a case.
why: The start of the mobile phone; it reaches Swiss pockets with Natel C (1987) and Natel D (1993).

title: Live Aid, and Boris Becker wins Wimbledon at 17
what: On 13 July concerts at Wembley in London and in Philadelphia raised money for famine relief in Ethiopia and were watched by an estimated 1.9 billion people. Earlier in July the unseeded West German Boris Becker beat Kevin Curren in the Wimbledon final. At 17 years and 227 days he is the youngest men's champion ever and the first German to win the title.
why: Two events of the summer of 1985 that a family in German-speaking Switzerland watched together; tennis fever follows.

title: Back to the Future opens in cinemas
what: Back to the Future opened in American cinemas on 3 July and took 11.3 million dollars in its first weekend, the most of any film. Michael J. Fox plays a teenager who travels back to 1955 in a time machine built from a DeLorean car.
why: The family film of the 1980s; already a colour item in the 1985 news.

title: Top Gun opens
what: Top Gun, starring Tom Cruise as a US Navy fighter pilot, opened in 1,028 American cinemas on 16 May. Reviews were mixed; critics praised the flying scenes and the soundtrack.
why: The blockbuster, the sunglasses and the bomber jackets of 1986.

title: Maradona's Argentina win the World Cup
what: Argentina beat West Germany 3-2 in the World Cup final in Mexico City on 29 June. In the quarter-final against England on 22 June Diego Maradona scored both goals, one of them with his hand.
why: The football summer of 1986 and its most famous player; already a colour item in the 1986 news.

title: A German teenager lands a small plane next to Red Square
what: On 28 May Mathias Rust, an 18-year-old amateur pilot from West Germany with about 50 hours of flying experience, landed a rented Cessna on a bridge next to Red Square in Moscow. He had flown from Helsinki through Soviet air defences without being stopped. He was arrested two hours later.
why: A teenager making fools of the Soviet military: the kind of story the family's teenagers would retell.

title: Dirty Dancing opens
what: The dance film Dirty Dancing, with Patrick Swayze and Jennifer Grey, opened in American cinemas on 21 August. The small studio Vestron made it on a low budget.
why: The film every teenager of 1987 saw, with a soundtrack that played at every party. Review 2026-10: cut 'its executives expected a flop', a later anecdote.

title: Nintendo's Game Boy goes on sale in Japan
what: Nintendo released the Game Boy, a hand-held game machine, in Japan on 21 April for 12,500 yen. It has a black-and-white screen and runs for up to 30 hours on four AA batteries. It is due in America in the summer.
why: The toy of a generation; Nintendo is not in the game, so no asset. Already a colour item in the 1989 news.

title: Zurich's S-Bahn starts running
what: Zurich's S-Bahn began running on 27 May, with a new tunnel under the city and new stations. The main lines run every half hour. From the same day one ticket from the new Zurich transport association, the ZVV, is valid on S-Bahn trains, express trains, buses and trams.
why: Commuting in the Zurich region changes for good; suburbs grow along the lines.

title: West Germany win the World Cup in Italy
what: West Germany beat Argentina 1-0 in the World Cup final in Rome on 8 July, through a late penalty by Andreas Brehme. It is their third title, won as the two Germanies prepare to unite.
why: Italia 90, the World Cup of the summer when Germany came together.

title: Jurassic Park breaks the box-office record
what: Steven Spielberg's Jurassic Park opened in American cinemas on 11 June and took 50.1 million dollars in its first weekend, a new record. Its dinosaurs were made with computer-generated images by Industrial Light & Magic and with life-sized animatronic models.
why: The dinosaur summer of 1993 for the family's children.

title: Toy Story, the first film made entirely by computer
what: Toy Story, made by Steve Jobs's Pixar and released by Disney, opened in American cinemas on 22 November and set a record for its opening weekend. It is the first feature film made entirely by computer animation. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voice a cowboy doll and a space ranger toy.
why: A new kind of film; the Disney-Pixar partnership leads to Disney buying Pixar in 2006.

title: The summer of the Macarena, and a phone that sends e-mail
what: The Macarena, a Spanish song with a dance that everyone can do, reached number one in the American charts in August and its dance has become a craze. On 15 August Nokia put on sale the 9000 Communicator, a mobile phone that opens like a small laptop with a keyboard and can send faxes and e-mail; in Britain it costs about 1,000 pounds.
why: A fad and a gadget: the phone as an office in the pocket, ten years before the smartphone.

title: Princess Diana dies in a Paris car crash
what: Diana, Princess of Wales, died after a car crash in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel in Paris in the night of 30 to 31 August, aged 36. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the driver were killed too. The car had been followed by photographers. Flowers are piling up outside her London home, Kensington Palace.
why: The most-watched news story of the late 1990s; her funeral on 6 September draws a huge television audience.

title: A new Star Wars film, sixteen years on
what: Star Wars: Episode I, The Phantom Menace opened in American cinemas on 19 May, almost 16 years after Return of the Jedi. Its premiere was covered by media around the world.
why: The parents of the game saw the first films as children; now they take their own.

title: The 'I love you' virus
what: From 4 May an e-mail with the subject 'ILOVEYOU' spread around the world, first in Asia, then in Europe as people arrived at work, then in America. Its attachment, a computer worm, overwrites files and sends itself to everyone in the victim's address book. Companies shut down their e-mail systems. It was traced to the Philippines.
why: E-mail has become part of office life, and so has its danger.

title: Brigitte McMahon wins the first Olympic triathlon
what: At the Olympics in Sydney, Brigitte McMahon of Baar won the first Olympic women's triathlon in 2 hours, 0 minutes and 40 seconds.
why: A Swiss gold at the far side of the world.

title: The PlayStation 2 reaches Europe
what: Sony's PlayStation 2 went on sale in Europe on 24 November, after Japan in March and North America in October. It plays the old PlayStation games and also DVD films, and, as in America, supplies are short.
why: Sony's console of the 2000s; the DVD arrives in many homes with it.

title: Young Roger Federer beats Sampras at Wimbledon
what: The 19-year-old Roger Federer of Basel beat Pete Sampras, the four-time defending champion, in five sets in the fourth round at Wimbledon, ending Sampras's run of 31 wins there. Federer then lost in the quarter-finals. He was Wimbledon junior champion in 1998.
why: The first glimpse of the Swiss sportsman of the age; his story runs to 2022.

title: Apple's iPod: '1,000 songs in your pocket'
what: On 23 October Apple presented the iPod, a music player with a 5 GB hard drive that holds about 1,000 songs, works with Apple's iTunes software on the Mac, and is controlled with a scroll wheel. It goes on sale on 10 November for 399 dollars, a lot for a music player.
why: The successor to the Walkman and the start of Apple's rise from computer maker to the world's most valuable company.

title: Harry Potter comes to the cinema
what: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, the film of J. K. Rowling's first book about a boy wizard, opened in Britain and America on 16 November. It is released by Warner Bros.
why: The children's craze of the 2000s, in books and films.

title: Euro notes and coins in the neighbouring countries
what: On 1 January euro notes and coins went into circulation in twelve EU countries, among them Germany, France, Italy and Austria. The mark, the French franc, the lira and the schilling can be exchanged until the end of February. The euro has existed since 1999, but only for accounts and electronic payments. Switzerland keeps its franc, but Swiss travellers and shoppers across the border now meet one currency on three sides.
why: For Swiss travellers and shoppers across the border, one currency replaces the mark, franc, lira and schilling.

title: Simon Ammann's double gold in Salt Lake City
what: At the Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City, the 20-year-old Swiss ski jumper Simon Ammann won both individual events, on the normal and the large hill, weeks after a crash in training. With his glasses and boyish face he is being compared to Harry Potter, and he appeared on David Letterman's American talk show.
why: An unexpected Swiss star of the winter of 2002.

title: Expo.02, the Swiss national exhibition, opens on the lakes
what: Switzerland's sixth national exhibition, Expo.02, opened on 15 May and runs until 20 October. It is spread over four 'Arteplages' built for the event on the lake shores at Biel, Murten, Neuchâtel and Yverdon-les-Bains, plus a converted gravel barge that travels between them. It was planned for 2001 and postponed by a year.
why: A summer outing for Swiss families, and a once-a-generation event.

title: Alinghi wins the America's Cup for landlocked Switzerland
what: On 2 March the Geneva yacht Alinghi, owned by Ernesto Bertarelli and skippered by New Zealander Russell Coutts, won the America's Cup in Auckland, beating Team New Zealand five races to none. Switzerland, without a coastline, now holds sailing's oldest trophy.
why: A Swiss sporting oddity that made headlines worldwide; Alinghi defends the cup in 2007.

title: Apple opens the iTunes Music Store
what: Apple opened its iTunes Music Store on 28 April, selling songs for download for 99 cents each, at first only to Mac users in the United States. All five major record companies, fighting free file-sharing, have agreed to sell through it.
why: The legal way to buy digital music, and the iPod's partner.

title: Federer wins Wimbledon
what: Roger Federer won Wimbledon in early July, beating Mark Philippoussis in the final after beating Andy Roddick in the semi-final. At 21 it is his first Grand Slam title and the first by a Swiss man.
why: The start of the Federer years, which colour Swiss summers for two decades.

title: Heatwave: Switzerland passes 40 degrees for the first time
what: On 11 August Grono in the Misox valley measured 41.5 degrees, the first temperature above 40 ever recorded in Switzerland, beating the old record of 39 degrees from 1952. The summer of 2003 is the hottest on record across much of Europe, and in France thousands of old people have died in the heat.
why: The summer that put climate change into everyday conversation.

title: Federer wins in Melbourne and becomes world number one
what: Roger Federer won the Australian Open on 1 February, beating Marat Safin in the final, and with it became the world's number one tennis player for the first time. It is his second Grand Slam title after Wimbledon last July. He is 22.
why: The start of Federer's long reign at the top; Swiss sport has a global star.

title: Google offers free e-mail with a whole gigabyte
what: On 1 April Google launched Gmail, a free e-mail service with one gigabyte of storage per user, a significantly higher amount than competitors offer.
why: E-mail moves to the web; free storage and online services become part of everyday life.

title: Greece win Euro 2004
what: Greece won the European Championship in Portugal on 4 July, beating the hosts 1-0 in the final with a goal by Angelos Charisteas, as they had in the opening match. Before the tournament Greece had qualified for only two major tournaments. Switzerland went out in the group stage; its only goal came from 18-year-old Johan Vonlanthen, the youngest scorer in the history of the European Championship.
why: The great football surprise of the decade.

title: Bahn 2000: Swiss trains every half hour
what: On 12 December the Swiss railways opened the new line between Mattstetten and Rothrist, the heart of the Bahn 2000 project, with the biggest timetable change in decades. Most intercity routes now run every half hour, and the trip from Zurich to Bern is 13 minutes shorter. The first stage cost 5.9 billion francs.
why: Daily commuting in Switzerland changes again; the clock-face timetable of 1982 gets denser.

title: Floods in central Switzerland
what: After days of heavy rain, floods and landslides hit central Switzerland and the Bernese Oberland around 22 August. Engelberg, with 4,000 inhabitants and 1,000 tourists, was cut off and could only be reached by helicopter, and two firemen were killed in the Entlebuch by a landslide. Six to ten people died in Switzerland, and damage runs into billions of francs.
why: The 'flood of the century' that many Swiss families remember; insurers count 2.5 billion francs of damage in October.

title: Switzerland qualify for the World Cup in Istanbul
what: Switzerland qualified for next summer's World Cup in Germany by beating Turkey in a play-off in November: 4-4 on aggregate, with the Swiss going through on away goals after the second leg in Istanbul. It is their first World Cup since 1994.
why: Sets up the football summer of 2006, the first big tournament next door.

title: World Cup in Germany: the Swiss go out without conceding a goal
what: At the World Cup in Germany, Switzerland drew 0-0 with France, beat Togo and South Korea 2-0 each and won its group. In the round of 16 on 26 June it lost to Ukraine on penalties after a 0-0 draw, missing all three of its penalties. Switzerland is the first team ever to leave a World Cup without conceding a goal.
why: The 'summer fairy tale' next door that Swiss families shared on public screens.

title: Google buys YouTube
what: Google completed its purchase of YouTube on 13 November for 1.65 billion dollars. The video-sharing site was registered in February 2005, and its first video, 'Me at the zoo', went online in April 2005; now people upload huge numbers of home-made clips every day.
why: Video moves from the television to the internet; the teenagers of the game grow up on it.

title: Nintendo's Wii: games you play by moving
what: Nintendo's Wii console reached Europe in December, after North America in November. Its wireless controller senses movement, so players swing their arms to play tennis or bowling.
why: The console that brought the whole family in front of the screen; Nintendo is not in the game.

title: Apple presents the iPhone
what: On 9 January Steve Jobs presented the iPhone at the Macworld conference in San Francisco: a mobile phone, an iPod and an internet device in one, with almost no buttons and a 3.5-inch touch screen worked with the fingers. It will go on sale in the United States in June. Apple Computer is also dropping 'Computer' from its name.
why: The device that ends the era of Nokia and starts the smartphone age; the core of Apple's later fortune.

title: The last Harry Potter book, and Alinghi keeps the America's Cup
what: On 21 July the seventh and final Harry Potter book, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, went on sale and set sales records in its first 24 hours. On 3 July in Valencia the Swiss yacht Alinghi defended the America's Cup against Team New Zealand, winning 5-2, the last race by one second.
why: A childhood ends for the Potter generation; Swiss sailing keeps its trophy.

title: Euro 2008 in Switzerland and Austria
what: Switzerland and Austria hosted the European Championship from 7 to 29 June. Switzerland opened the tournament in Basel and lost to the Czech Republic, then to Turkey, and was the first team out, though it beat Portugal in its last game; captain Alexander Frei was injured in the first match. Spain won the final in Vienna, 1-0 against Germany.
why: A once-in-a-lifetime home tournament, with fan zones in Swiss cities.

title: The iPhone 3G and the App Store
what: On 11 July Apple released the iPhone 3G in 22 countries. A day earlier it opened the App Store, where iPhone owners can download programs from other companies; it started with 500 apps.
why: The smartphone arrives in Swiss pockets; apps become a new industry.

title: Beijing Olympics: Federer and Wawrinka win doubles gold
what: At the Olympics in Beijing, Roger Federer and Stanislas Wawrinka won gold in the men's tennis doubles, and Fabian Cancellara won the cycling time trial.
why: Swiss gold at a Games watched for China's coming-out party.

title: Michael Jackson dies; Federer wins the French Open
what: Michael Jackson died in Los Angeles on 25 June, aged 50, weeks before a series of comeback concerts in London; the news brought unprecedented surges of internet traffic. Earlier in June Roger Federer finally won the French Open, beating Robin Söderling in the final, which gives him all four Grand Slam titles and equals Pete Sampras's record of 14.
why: The pop death of the decade, and the high point of Federer's career, followed in July by a record 15th title at Wimbledon.

title: Switzerland's under-17s win the World Cup
what: Switzerland won the under-17 World Cup in Nigeria on 15 November, beating the hosts and holders Nigeria 1-0 in the final. Goalkeeper Benjamin Siegrist won the award for best goalkeeper, and Haris Seferovic was among the top scorers.
why: The first Swiss football world title; a sign of the generation that later plays for the national team.

title: Avatar and the 3D cinema
what: James Cameron's Avatar opened in American cinemas on 18 December, filmed with new motion-capture techniques and shown in 3D, with glasses. Its release was pushed back partly to give cinemas time to install 3D projectors, and 2,032 of the 3,457 American cinemas showing it do so in 3D. Its production cost has been put at roughly 300 million dollars.
why: The blockbuster of the season; 3D television never caught on.

title: Simon Ammann's double gold again, in Vancouver
what: At the Winter Olympics in Vancouver, Simon Ammann won both individual ski jumping events, as he did in 2002. He is the first athlete to win both individual jumping golds at two Games and is now the most successful Swiss Olympian.
why: A Swiss winter hero for a second time.

title: Volcanic ash from Iceland grounds Europe's planes
what: After the Eyjafjallajökull volcano in Iceland erupted on 14 April, its ash cloud drifted over Europe, and much of European airspace was closed from 15 April for nearly a week, for fear the ash would damage jet engines. Over 95,000 flights were cancelled and millions of passengers were stranded.
why: The Easter holidays that ended in chaos; a reminder of how much daily life depends on flying.

title: The iPad goes on sale in Switzerland
what: Apple's iPad, a tablet computer with a 9.7-inch touch screen, went on sale in Switzerland, Germany, France, Britain and five other countries on 28 May, after the United States in April. The base model costs 499 dollars in the US, less than analysts had expected.
why: The tablet joins the smartphone; grandparents who never used a computer start reading news on one.

title: Switzerland beat Spain at the World Cup
what: In their first game at the World Cup in South Africa, Switzerland beat European champions Spain 1-0 in Durban on 16 June, with a goal by Gelson Fernandes. They then lost to Chile and drew with Honduras, and went out in the group stage.
why: A famous Swiss win against the team that went on to become world champion.

title: Prince William marries Catherine Middleton
what: Prince William married Catherine Middleton at Westminster Abbey on 29 April. About a million people lined the route in London, and tens of millions watched around the world, 72 million of them on live streams on YouTube.
why: A royal wedding for a new generation, thirty years after Charles and Diana's.

title: The strong franc makes shopping across the border cheap
what: From May 2010 to early August 2011 the Swiss franc rose by more than 30 per cent against the euro, as investors fled the euro debt crisis. For Swiss families, holidays abroad and the shops in Germany, France and Italy have become much cheaper, while the export industry at home suffers. Shoppers can also reclaim German VAT.
why: Cross-border shopping becomes a Saturday habit in Swiss border regions; the SNB caps the franc in September.

title: Steve Jobs dies
what: Steve Jobs, the co-founder of Apple, died on 5 October aged 56, six weeks after stepping down as chief executive. He was behind the Macintosh, the iPod, the iPhone and the iPad.
why: The end of an era for the company that defined the gadgets of the game.

title: Federer's seventh Wimbledon
what: Roger Federer beat Andy Murray in the Wimbledon final, his seventh Wimbledon title and 17th Grand Slam title, equalling the records of Pete Sampras and William Renshaw. With the win he is world number one again, at almost 31.
why: Federer's last major title for almost five years.

title: A skydiver breaks the sound barrier, live on YouTube
what: On 14 October the Austrian Felix Baumgartner jumped from a capsule about 39 kilometres above New Mexico, carried up by a helium balloon, and became the first person to break the sound barrier without an engine, reaching about 1,358 kilometres per hour. More than 9.5 million people watched live on YouTube, a record. The project was paid for by Red Bull.
why: Watching events live online, not on television, becomes normal.

title: Gangnam Style passes a billion views
what: On 21 December the video of 'Gangnam Style' by the South Korean singer Psy became the first YouTube video to reach a billion views. Since its release in July its horse-riding dance has spawned parodies and reaction videos around the world.
why: The first global internet hit; K-pop arrives in Europe.

title: Breaking Bad ends; series are binged on Netflix
what: The American series Breaking Bad, about a chemistry teacher who becomes a drug maker, ended on 29 September after five seasons. Its audience grew as viewers caught up on earlier seasons on Netflix, and the finale was one of the most-watched cable episodes of recent years.
why: Television becomes something you watch when you like, many episodes at a time.

title: Sony's PlayStation 4
what: Sony launched the PlayStation 4 in North America on 15 November and in Europe on 29 November, at 399 euros. Sony wants to avoid the mistakes of the PlayStation 3, which came a year after Microsoft's Xbox 360.
why: A success for Sony's game business, which carries the company in the 2010s.

title: Stan Wawrinka wins the Australian Open
what: Stan Wawrinka beat Rafael Nadal in the final of the Australian Open, his first Grand Slam title, after beating world number two Novak Djokovic on the way. Switzerland now has two Grand Slam champions.
why: Federer is no longer the only Swiss tennis winner; it leads to the Davis Cup in November.

title: Sochi: Dario Cologna wins two golds
what: At the Winter Olympics in Sochi, the cross-country skier Dario Cologna won the 30-kilometre skiathlon and the 15-kilometre classic race, defending his Olympic title from Vancouver.
why: A Swiss winter star from a sport not usually Swiss.

title: Netflix arrives in Switzerland
what: In September the American streaming service Netflix started in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Belgium and Luxembourg. For a monthly fee it shows films and series over the internet, whenever the viewer wants.
why: The end of fixed television schedules for the family's younger members.

title: Federer and Wawrinka win the Davis Cup
what: Switzerland won tennis's Davis Cup for the first time, beating France in the final in Lille from 21 to 23 November. Roger Federer and Stan Wawrinka led the team.
why: A national team title in tennis, rare for a small country.

title: Wawrinka wins the French Open
what: Stan Wawrinka beat world number one Novak Djokovic in the French Open final, his second Grand Slam title. On the way he also beat Roger Federer.
why: Swiss tennis at its peak, with two Grand Slam winners.

title: Paying by phone: Twint starts across Switzerland
what: Twint, an app from PostFinance for paying with a smartphone and sending money to friends, started its national rollout on 3 November after a trial in Bern and Zurich in August. A rival app, Paymit, comes from UBS, the Zürcher Kantonalbank and the stock exchange operator SIX.
why: The start of mobile payment in Switzerland; the two apps merge in 2016 and Twint becomes the way the Swiss pay each other.

title: Star Wars returns, now made by Disney
what: Star Wars: The Force Awakens opened on 18 December, the first Star Wars film since Disney bought Lucasfilm from George Lucas in 2012, and broke box-office records in its first days. Harrison Ford, Carrie Fisher and Mark Hamill return.
why: Three generations in the family have now seen a Star Wars film in the cinema.

title: The Gotthard Base Tunnel opens
what: The Gotthard Base Tunnel was inaugurated on 1 June. At 57 kilometres it is the longest railway tunnel in the world, the first flat, low-level route through the Alps, for trains between central Switzerland and Ticino. Regular service begins in December.
why: A Swiss engineering pride of the century and a change for travel to Ticino and Italy.

title: Solar Impulse flies round the world; Pokémon Go sends players into the streets
what: On 26 July the Swiss solar-powered plane Solar Impulse 2, flown by Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg, landed in Abu Dhabi, completing the first flight around the world on solar power alone after 16 months. Since 6 July the smartphone game Pokémon Go has had millions of people walking through towns to catch virtual creatures on their screens; it was downloaded more than 10 million times in its first week.
why: A Swiss pioneering feat, and a summer when the phone game left the sofa.

title: Federer's comeback: the Australian Open at 35
what: Roger Federer beat Rafael Nadal in five sets in the Australian Open final, his 18th Grand Slam title and his first since 2012. He had missed half of 2016 after knee surgery. At 35 he is the oldest Grand Slam men's champion since 1972.
why: A comeback that the whole family followed; Wimbledon follows in July.

title: Federer's record eighth Wimbledon
what: Roger Federer beat Marin Čilić in the Wimbledon final without losing a set all tournament, his record eighth Wimbledon title and 19th Grand Slam title.
why: Federer's record at the tournament he loved most.

title: Federer wins his 20th Grand Slam title
what: Roger Federer won the Australian Open again, the first man to win 20 Grand Slam singles titles. He is 36.
why: The last of Federer's Grand Slam titles.

title: The 'eagle' goals against Serbia
what: At the World Cup in Russia, Switzerland drew 1-1 with Brazil and beat Serbia 2-1 with a late goal by Xherdan Shaqiri. Shaqiri and Granit Xhaka, both of Albanian descent, celebrated their goals with a double-headed eagle gesture, the Albanian emblem, which caused a controversy; FIFA did not ban them.
why: A debate about identity in a Swiss team built by immigrant families.

title: Swiss pupils strike for the climate
what: On 17 and 18 January at least 45,000 students in Switzerland and Germany skipped school to protest against weak climate policies, following the Swedish schoolgirl Greta Thunberg, who began the school strikes outside her country's parliament. More strikes are planned.
why: The teenagers of the game take to the streets; climate dominates the Swiss election year.

title: Women's strike again, 28 years later
what: On 14 June an estimated 500,000 people joined a nationwide women's strike in Switzerland, the second after 1991, demanding equal pay, protection against harassment and more women in politics. Many wore purple and marched in Bern, Zurich, Basel, Geneva and Lausanne.
why: Daughters join their mothers; four months later a record number of women are elected to parliament.

title: Disney+ starts streaming
what: Disney launched its streaming service Disney+ on 12 November in the United States, Canada and the Netherlands, with films and series from Disney, Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars. It plans to roll it out worldwide over the next two years.
why: Disney takes on Netflix; the streaming wars begin.

title: Switzerland shuts down
what: On 16 March the Federal Council declared an 'extraordinary situation' under the epidemics law because of the coronavirus. Schools, shops other than food stores, restaurants and bars are closed, and from 20 March gatherings of more than five people are banned. Many parents work from home. Disney+ started in Switzerland on 24 March, just in time.
why: The most sudden change in daily life in the game: home office, home schooling, video calls.

title: Masks on trains and buses
what: From July masks became mandatory on public transport in Switzerland. Shops and schools reopened in May, and most of the spring measures have been lifted step by step, but the virus has not gone away.
why: The mask becomes an everyday object for every generation.

title: The first vaccinations
what: On 23 December Switzerland began vaccinating against COVID-19, four days after the regulator Swissmedic approved the first vaccine. Restaurants, sports and cultural venues have been closed again since the cases rose in the autumn.
why: The grandparents are first in line.

title: Switzerland knock world champions France out of the Euro
what: At the European Championship, held a year late because of the pandemic, Switzerland came back from 1-3 down to draw 3-3 with world champions France on 28 June and won on penalties. It is Switzerland's first knockout win at a major tournament since 1938. They meet Spain in the quarter-final.
why: The football night of the pandemic years; crowds celebrated in Swiss streets.

title: Belinda Bencic wins Olympic gold in Tokyo
what: At the Olympics in Tokyo, held a year late without spectators, Belinda Bencic won the women's tennis tournament, the biggest title of her career, and a silver medal in the doubles.
why: A Swiss gold at the Games of the pandemic.

title: The Covid certificate for restaurants, and Squid Game
what: From 13 September a Covid certificate, proof of vaccination, recovery or a negative test shown as a QR code on the phone, is needed to enter restaurants, bars, museums and gyms in Switzerland. On 17 September Netflix released the South Korean series Squid Game, which is drawing international attention.
why: The phone becomes an entry ticket; and a Korean series becomes a world event.

title: Switzerland lifts almost all Covid rules
what: On 17 February Switzerland lifted almost all its coronavirus measures. The certificate is no longer needed, and masks remain mandatory only on public transport and in healthcare institutions.
why: The end of two years of restrictions; home office stays.

title: Roger Federer retires
what: On 15 September Roger Federer, 41, announced that he will retire from professional tennis after the Laver Cup later this month, a team competition he helped create. He won 20 Grand Slam titles and was the first man to reach 20. He had played little since knee operations.
why: The end of the Swiss sporting story that ran through two decades of the game.

title: ChatGPT, and Messi's World Cup
what: ChatGPT, a chatbot from the American company OpenAI that answers questions and writes texts in ordinary language, was released on 30 November and gained one million users in five days. On 18 December Argentina won the World Cup final in Qatar against France on penalties after a 3-3 draw, with two goals by Lionel Messi and a hat-trick by Kylian Mbappé.
why: Artificial intelligence enters homes and schools; the Messi final is watched by a record television audience.

title: Apple shows the Vision Pro headset
what: On 5 June Apple presented the Vision Pro, a headset worn over the eyes that shows apps and films floating in the room around the user, filmed by its cameras. It is due in the United States early next year for 3,499 dollars.
why: Apple's bet on the next device after the phone; it stays a niche.

title: Barbenheimer
what: On 21 July two very different films opened on the same day: Barbie, a pink comedy about the doll, and Oppenheimer, a three-hour drama about the father of the atomic bomb. Online, the pairing became the 'Barbenheimer' phenomenon, with people planning to see both.
why: A summer when people went back to the cinema.

title: Nemo wins Eurovision for Switzerland
what: The Swiss singer Nemo won the Eurovision Song Contest in Malmö on 11 May with 'The Code', winning the combined and the jury vote. Nemo is the first openly non-binary winner. Switzerland will host the contest next year.
why: A Swiss pop moment that the family discussed, and the 2025 contest comes to Basel.

title: Switzerland knock out holders Italy at Euro 2024
what: At the European Championship in Germany, Switzerland beat the defending champions Italy in the round of 16 and reached the quarter-finals for the second tournament in a row.
why: Another Swiss football summer next door.

title: Eurovision in Basel
what: The Eurovision Song Contest was held at the St. Jakobshalle in Basel, with the final on 17 May, presented by Hazel Brugger, Sandra Studer and Michelle Hunziker. It is the third time Switzerland has hosted it, after Lugano in 1956 and Lausanne in 1989. Austria's JJ won with 'Wasted Love'.
why: A week of pop in Basel.

title: Women's Euro in Switzerland
what: Switzerland hosted the women's European football championship from 2 to 27 July, with the opening match and the final in Basel. A record 657,291 spectators came to the games. England kept their title, beating Spain on penalties in the final.
why: Women's football fills Swiss stadiums; the daughters of the game have new role models.

title: Franjo von Allmen's three golds at Milano Cortina
what: At the Winter Olympics in Milan and Cortina d'Ampezzo, from 6 to 22 February, Franjo von Allmen won the downhill, the super-G and the team combined with Tanguy Nef, the first alpine skier with three golds at one Games since 2002. Loïc Meillard won the slalom, Mathilde Gremaud the freeski slopestyle and Marianne Fatton the first Olympic ski mountaineering sprint. Switzerland won six golds and 23 medals in all.
why: The best Swiss Winter Games in a generation, next door in Italy.

title: Switzerland reach a World Cup quarter-final for the first time since 1954
what: At the World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico, Switzerland won its group, then beat Colombia on penalties after a goalless game, with a save by Gregor Kobel and the winning penalty by Rubén Vargas. It was their first World Cup quarter-final since 1954. There they lost to Argentina, after Breel Embolo was sent off. Spain won the final against Argentina 1-0 after extra time on 19 July.
why: The best Swiss World Cup in 72 years, at the end of the game's span.
